stages.title: Advanced logic and reasoning
stages.hook: "Everyone loves someone" and "Someone is loved by everyone" look similar. Are they the same claim?
explain: Predicate (first-order) logic extends propositional logic with variables, predicates and quantifiers. ∀x P(x) says P holds for all x in the domain; ∃x P(x) says it holds for at least one. Negation swaps quantifiers: ¬∀x P(x) ≡ ∃x ¬P(x), and ¬∃x P(x) ≡ ∀x ¬P(x). Order matters: ∀x ∃y Loves(x,y) ("everyone loves someone") does not entail ∃y ∀x Loves(x,y) ("there is someone whom everyone loves"), but the second entails the first.

A formal system has syntax (formulas), semantics (interpretations that assign truth) and proof rules. Soundness means whatever is provable is semantically valid; completeness means whatever is semantically valid is provable. Gödel's completeness theorem (1929) shows that first-order logic is complete. His incompleteness theorems (1931) show that any consistent, effectively axiomatised system strong enough for basic arithmetic contains true statements it cannot prove, and cannot prove its own consistency. Church and Turing showed that validity in first-order logic is undecidable: no algorithm decides it for all formulas.

Proof techniques: direct proof, contrapositive, contradiction (reductio ad absurdum), induction and counterexample. A single counterexample refutes a universal claim; no number of examples proves one. Induction proves a statement for all natural numbers by proving a base case and the step from n to n + 1. Example: 1 + 2 + … + n = n(n+1)/2 holds for n = 1 and, if true for n, adding n + 1 gives (n+1)(n+2)/2.

example.q: Show that √2 is irrational by contradiction (outline).
steps: Suppose √2 = a/b in lowest terms, so a² = 2b².
Then a² is even, so a is even; write a = 2c, giving 4c² = 2b², so b² = 2c².
Then b is even too, contradicting lowest terms.
example.a: The assumption leads to a contradiction, so √2 is irrational.

analogies.tech: A database query "for all users there exists an order" differs from "there exists an order for all users".
analogies.city: "Every road leads to some junction" versus "some junction is reached by every road".
analogies.home: "Each key opens some lock" versus "some lock is opened by every key".

stages.mnemonic: For all is a net, there exists is a hook; swap their order and change the book.
terms: A symbol (∀ or ∃) saying how many members of the domain satisfy a predicate.
Proof by showing that denial leads to contradiction.

misc.wrong: Gödel proved that mathematics is inconsistent or that nothing can be known.
misc.right: Gödel showed limits of formal systems: some true arithmetic statements are unprovable within a given consistent system. It does not make mathematics unreliable.

stages.limits: Philosophers debate what the incompleteness theorems imply about minds and machines; claims that they prove human minds exceed computers are contested.

trip.prompt: Read about what the first theorem states and what it does not.

Anecdote

teach.model: Predicate logic adds quantifiers: for all and there exists. Negating swaps them, and order matters. Soundness means provable implies valid; completeness means valid implies provable. Gödel showed limits of formal systems. Proof methods include contradiction and induction, and one counterexample refutes a universal claim.

points.ask: What happens when I change order or negate?
What are the limits of formal systems?
How can I prove or refute?

stages.title: Epistemological theories
stages.hook: You read a fact in a textbook, recall a childhood event and check a thermometer. Which of these gives knowledge, and what justifies each?
explain: Contemporary epistemology asks what justifies belief and how it relates to truth. Internalists hold that justification depends on factors accessible to the believer (such as evidence they can reflect upon); externalists allow factors the believer need not access, such as the reliability of the process producing the belief. A thermometer-like reliable process may yield knowledge even if the believer cannot explain why.

Further views. Contextualism says the standards for "knows" vary with the conversational context: in a casual chat "I know the bank is open" may be fine, but with high stakes we demand more. Virtue epistemology treats knowledge as success from intellectual virtue (competence). Bayesian epistemology models belief as degrees of credence updated by conditionalisation. Social epistemology studies testimony, expert authority and group knowledge: most of what we know comes from others, so trust and reliability of sources are central, and so are problems such as echo chambers and epistemic injustice.

Puzzles: the lottery paradox (for a 1000-ticket lottery you can be 99.9% sure each ticket loses, yet certain that some ticket wins, so full belief in each cannot all be rational), the regress of justification, and scepticism. Memory is a source with limits: reconstruction means false memories can feel vivid, and confidence is only weakly related to accuracy, which matters for eyewitness testimony. Responsible believers calibrate confidence to evidence and remain open to revision.

example.q: In a 1000-ticket fair lottery, what is the probability that a given ticket loses, and why is the lottery paradox puzzling?
steps: For each ticket, it seems rational to believe it will lose.
But then you believe all tickets lose, contradicting your belief that one wins.
example.a: 0.999; high probability alone does not seem enough for outright belief or knowledge.

analogies.city: You trust a map made by surveyors you will never meet (testimony).
analogies.tech: A search engine ranks sources; relying on it is reliance on others' reliability.
analogies.nature: A bird navigates by reliable magnetic sense without being able to explain it (an externalist analogy).

stages.mnemonic: Inside the head, or out in the world: where does justification lie?
terms: Justification depends on factors accessible to the believer.
Justification can depend on factors outside the believer's awareness, such as reliability.
The standards for knowledge claims vary with context.
A degree of belief between 0 and 1.

misc.wrong: Knowledge is just whatever is true and sincerely believed.
misc.right: Most accounts require something more: justification, reliability, or competence that links belief to truth.

stages.limits: The theories compete and each faces counterexamples; there is no consensus analysis of knowledge or justification.

trip.prompt: Find the main arguments for and against each view.

questions.q: An externalist about justification would say a belief can be justified if...

o: Factors accessible to the believer

questions.q: Contextualism holds that...

o: High probability may not suffice for outright belief or knowledge
Lotteries are unfair to those who buy tickets
Probabilities are meaningless when applied to belief
Evidence is worthless when the odds are very large
questions.why: Believing every ticket loses conflicts with knowing one wins.

questions.q: Social epistemology highlights that...
o: Much knowledge depends on trusting others
Individuals can know everything on their own
Testimony from others is useless as a source

o: Memory is reconstructive and confidence can persist when memory is wrong
Witnesses always lie when they are under pressure
Confidence is an exact measure of accuracy

questions.q: Match each theory to its core claim.
pairs: Knowledge is success from intellectual competence
Belief comes in degrees updated by evidence

questions.q: Put the epistemic steps in order for relying on a testimonial source.
items: Identify the source and its competence

questions.q: Explain why an echo chamber can reduce knowledge even if each member reports honestly.
questions.model: Members repeat the same views, so agreement looks like independent confirmation when it is not, which inflates confidence and shields beliefs from challenge.

panel.q: A person has a reliable perceptual system but no idea why. Internalists would say...
o: Her belief may lack justification because she cannot access reasons
She definitely knows, because her perception works well
She has no belief, since she cannot give reasons
Reliability is irrelevant to every philosopher

panel.q: Why does the lottery paradox challenge the idea that knowledge is just high probability?
panel.model: If high probability sufficed for knowing, we would know of each ticket that it loses, and so know that all lose, yet we know one wins, which is contradictory.

panel.q: Which is the best response to widely shared claims without independent sources?
o: Seek independent evidence and calibrate confidence
Believe them because so many people hold them
Reject them all without checking any
Share them widely to see what people say

teach.model: Internalists tie justification to what a believer can access; externalists allow reliable processes. Contextualism says standards vary with context. Virtue and Bayesian accounts, social epistemology and the lottery paradox show that knowledge is more than high probability. Memory is fallible and confidence is not accuracy.

points.ask: How reliable are memory and testimony?

stages.title: Advanced scientific inference
stages.hook: A theory predicts something, and the experiment disagrees. Is the theory dead, or could something else be wrong?
explain: Philosophers disagree about how science works. Popper held that scientific theories must be falsifiable: bold conjectures that risk refutation, with science progressing by eliminating errors. Kuhn argued that "normal science" works within a paradigm until anomalies accumulate and cause a revolution. Lakatos described research programmes with a hard core protected by auxiliary hypotheses. The Duhem–Quine thesis points out that tests involve bundles of hypotheses (the theory plus assumptions about instruments), so a failed prediction does not by logic alone tell which part is wrong. Underdetermination: different theories can fit the same data.

Statistical inference. Frequentist methods ask how often a procedure would err in repeated use (p-values, confidence intervals). Bayesian methods update probability of hypotheses given data. The likelihood ratio compares how well two hypotheses predict the data: with 8 heads in 10 tosses, the likelihood under p = 0.5 is 45/1024 ≈ 0.0439 and under p = 0.8 is 45 × 0.8⁸ × 0.2² ≈ 0.302, a ratio of about 6.9 favouring p = 0.8. A 95% confidence interval for a mean with known standard deviation σ and sample size n is approximately mean ± 1.96 σ/√n.

Good practice and its pitfalls: statistical power (probability of detecting a real effect) matters, since low-powered studies produce unreliable positive results; p-hacking and flexible analysis inflate false positives; pre-registration and replication improve reliability. Inference to the best explanation guides theory choice by virtues such as accuracy, scope, simplicity and consistency, but there is no algorithm for weighing them. Correlation analysis needs causal models, and models themselves are idealisations: "all models are wrong, but some are useful" (a saying attributed to the statistician George Box).

example.q: A sample of n = 25 has σ = 10 known and mean 50. What is the approximate 95% confidence interval?

analogies.nature: Astronomers found Neptune after anomalies in Uranus's orbit: they blamed an unseen planet, not Newton's law, an auxiliary hypothesis choice.
analogies.tech: A failing test in software could be a bug in the code or in the test; the bundle of assumptions matters.
analogies.sport: A new training method fails in a trial; was it the method, the measurement or the sample?

stages.mnemonic: Test the bundle, not just the bolt: the theory travels with its assumptions.
terms: The property that a theory could in principle be shown false by observation.
A framework of shared assumptions and methods in a scientific field (Kuhn).
Different theories can fit the same evidence.
The probability of detecting a real effect of a given size.

misc.wrong: A failed prediction automatically refutes a theory.
misc.right: Predictions depend on auxiliary assumptions, so scientists must decide where to place the blame (Duhem–Quine).

stages.limits: Philosophers of science still debate whether science progresses by falsification, paradigms, research programmes or something else, and Bayesian and frequentist statisticians disagree on foundations.

Data is useless for choosing between theories

Experiments are impossible in such cases

o: Pre-registering analyses
Trying many analyses and reporting the best
Dropping inconvenient data
Waiting for significance

pairs: Science advances by trying to refute bold conjectures
Normal science is punctuated by paradigm shifts
Research programmes with a protected hard core

questions.why: The test applies to the whole bundle.

o: A smaller effect, or none, is quite possible
Exactly the same effect, down to the last detail
A larger effect than the first study found
A certain success on every attempt

panel.q: Compare a frequentist confidence interval with a Bayesian credible interval in interpretation.
panel.model: A frequentist 95% confidence interval comes from a procedure that captures the true value in 95% of repeated samples, while a Bayesian credible interval states the posterior probability that the parameter lies in the interval given the data and prior.

panel.q: Neptune was predicted from anomalies in Uranus's orbit. What does this show about auxiliary assumptions?
o: Scientists can revise an auxiliary hypothesis and keep the theory
Newton's theory was simply refuted by the data
Anomalies are always errors and can be ignored
Observations are useless in testing theories
panel.why: Sometimes the correct response to an anomaly is a new auxiliary hypothesis.

teach.model: Popper stressed falsifiability, Kuhn paradigms, Lakatos research programmes. Duhem–Quine says tests involve bundles of assumptions, and data may underdetermine theory. Use likelihood ratios, intervals, power, pre-registration and replication to reduce errors.

points.ask: How do we make results reliable?

stages.title: Decision theory
stages.hook: Would you prefer a sure 36 coins or a coin flip for 100 or 0? Does your answer match the one with the higher expected value?
explain: Decision theory studies rational choice under uncertainty. Expected value (EV) is the probability-weighted average payoff. Expected utility theory (von Neumann and Morgenstern) says that if preferences satisfy certain axioms (completeness, transitivity, continuity, independence), then a decision maker acts as if maximising the expected value of a utility function u. If u is concave (like u(x) = √x), the person is risk averse.

Example: a gamble gives 100 with probability 0.5 and 0 otherwise. EV = 50. With u(x) = √x, expected utility = 0.5 × 10 + 0.5 × 0 = 5, equal to the utility of the certain amount 25 (since √25 = 5). The certainty equivalent is 25, so a sure 36 (utility 6) is preferred to the gamble. The St Petersburg paradox (a game with infinite expected payoff that nobody would pay much for) motivated diminishing marginal utility.

Descriptive findings contradict the axioms. In the Allais paradox people prefer a sure thing in one choice but a risky option in a second choice that differs from the first only by a common consequence added to both options, a pattern that violates the independence axiom. Prospect theory (Kahneman and Tversky) describes reference dependence, loss aversion (losses loom larger than equal gains, roughly by a factor of two) and probability weighting. Value of information: the expected value of perfect information (EVPI) is the gain from knowing the state before choosing. Normative theory tells us how to choose well given our values, but cannot say what to value; interpersonal comparisons and moral uncertainty remain debated.

example.q: State 1 (p = 0.5): A pays 100, B pays 40. State 2 (p = 0.5): A pays 0, B pays 40. Compute the expected value of perfect information.
steps: Without information: EV(A) = 50, EV(B) = 40, so choose A with 50.
With perfect information: in state 1 pick A (100), in state 2 pick B (40): 0.5 × 100 + 0.5 × 40 = 70.

analogies.farm: A farmer values a guaranteed modest crop more than a gamble with a higher average because a failed season could be ruinous.
analogies.sport: A team chooses a safe draw instead of a risky attack when the cost of defeat is high.
analogies.tech: A company pays for a pilot study to learn about demand before launching.

stages.mnemonic: Utility bends, gain and loss are not mirror images, and information has a price.
terms: The probability-weighted average of utilities of outcomes.
The sure amount valued the same as a gamble.
Losses weigh more heavily than equal-sized gains.

misc.wrong: A rational person must always maximise expected money.
misc.right: Utility can be concave in money, so risk aversion can be rational, and money is not the only value.

stages.limits: Whether the axioms of expected utility are requirements of rationality or only descriptive simplifications is debated, as is how to treat unknown probabilities.

trip.prompt: Find the St Petersburg paradox and how it was resolved.

o: Risk aversion
Risk seeking
Indifference to risk
No preferences

What is the certainty equivalent (in coins) of that gamble with u(x) = √x?

o: Losses hurt more than equal gains please
Gains hurt more than losses of the same size
Losses are ignored when we decide
Gains and losses feel exactly equal in size

questions.q: The St Petersburg paradox motivated...
o: Diminishing marginal utility
Bayes' theorem for updating beliefs
The Nash equilibrium of a game
The idea of loss aversion in choice
questions.why: A finite price despite infinite EV.

questions.q: Which axiom is violated by the Allais paradox choices?
o: Independence
Completeness
Transitivity of identity
Continuity of time
questions.why: The pattern conflicts with the independence axiom.

Why would a firm not pay more than the EVPI for any information?
o: Information cannot be worth more than perfect information
Information is always free to obtain
Information is always worth less than half the EVPI
The EVPI is a negative number
questions.why: Perfect information is the upper bound.

questions.q: Match each concept to its meaning.
pairs: Sure amount equal in value to a gamble
Outcomes judged as gains or losses relative to a point
Common outcomes should not change preferences

questions.q: Explain why risk aversion can be rational even when a gamble has a higher expected value.
questions.model: The extra money from a win may add less utility than the loss costs, especially if a loss threatens essentials, so a sure outcome can have higher expected utility than the gamble.
questions.why: Utility is not linear in money.

panel.q: Option A: 80 sure. Option B: 50% chance of 200, 50% of 0. With u(x) = √x which gives higher expected utility?
o: B, since its expected value is higher in money
They are equal, since both have the same expected value
The comparison cannot be computed from this

panel.q: Why can framing the same options as gains or as losses change choices, and what does this imply for rational choice theory?
panel.model: People respond differently to equivalent descriptions, violating the principle that equivalent options should be treated the same, so actual choice departs from the normative theory.

panel.q: A decision maker has unknown probabilities. Which is true?
o: Expected utility needs probabilities, so other rules such as maximin may be considered
Expected value always applies, however unclear the odds
No decision is possible without probabilities
The probabilities are always known in real life

teach.model: Expected utility theory says rational agents maximise expected utility. Concave utility explains risk aversion; the certainty equivalent measures it. Prospect theory describes loss aversion and framing. The expected value of perfect information bounds what information is worth.

points.ask: Why can people prefer a sure thing?

stages.title: Advanced game theory
stages.hook: In matching pennies, one player wants to match and the other wants to mismatch. Is there any stable pure strategy?
explain: Beyond dominant strategies, games can have Nash equilibria in mixed strategies, where players randomise. In matching pennies there is no pure equilibrium, since whoever is being outguessed wants to switch. The unique equilibrium has each player choose heads with probability 1/2, making the opponent indifferent. Nash proved that every finite game has at least one equilibrium in mixed strategies.

Coordination games have multiple equilibria. In Battle of the Sexes the payoffs are (2,1) if both choose Opera, (1,2) if both choose Fight, and 0 otherwise. Besides two pure equilibria there is a mixed one where the row player chooses Opera with probability 2/3 (making the column player indifferent: p × 1 = (1 − p) × 2 gives p = 2/3). The stag hunt contrasts a risk-dominant safe option with a payoff-dominant cooperative option.

Dynamic games use extensive form and backward induction. In the ultimatum game with a pot of 10 divided in whole units, backward induction predicts the proposer offers the minimum positive amount and the responder accepts; experiments show people often reject low offers, so models include fairness. Subgame-perfect equilibrium refines Nash by requiring optimal play in every subgame, removing non-credible threats. In repeated games, cooperation can be sustained: with grim trigger in a prisoner's dilemma with payoffs T = 5, R = 3, P = 1, S = 0, cooperation holds if the discount factor δ ≥ (T − R)/(T − P) = 0.5. The folk theorem says many outcomes can be equilibria in infinitely repeated games. Evolutionary game theory replaces rationality with selection: an evolutionarily stable strategy resists invasion.

example.q: Derive the discount factor threshold for grim-trigger cooperation with T = 5, R = 3, P = 1.
steps: Defecting now then mutual defection: 5 + δ × 1/(1 − δ).
Cooperate if 3 ≥ 5(1 − δ) + δ = 5 − 4δ, which gives δ ≥ 0.5.

analogies.sport: A penalty taker and goalkeeper mix their choices of corner so as not to be predictable.
analogies.city: Two firms deciding on a standard (like a plug type) face a coordination game.
analogies.nature: Animals contesting a resource can follow stable mixes of aggressive and peaceful behaviour (evolutionarily stable strategies).

stages.mnemonic: Mix to be unreadable, chain to be credible, wait to be kind.
terms: A strategy that randomises over actions with set probabilities.
Solving a sequential game from the last move backwards.
An equilibrium that is a Nash equilibrium in every subgame.
A strategy that cannot be invaded by a rare mutant strategy.

misc.wrong: Nash equilibria are always the best outcomes for the players.
misc.right: Equilibria can be bad for all, as in the prisoner's dilemma, and a game can have several.

stages.limits: Real behaviour often departs from equilibrium predictions, and the models assume known payoffs and common knowledge of rationality, which are strong assumptions.

questions.q: In matching pennies, the mixed-strategy equilibrium is...

Both players always play heads
No equilibrium exists in this game
The matcher always plays tails

What does backward induction require?
o: Solving from the last move back to the first
Randomising each move at the start of the game
Ignoring the later moves of the game
Making sure that all payoffs are equal
questions.why: Each earlier move anticipates later play.

Always effective, since it scares the other player
A mixed strategy used by the threatener
A dominant strategy for the threatener

questions.q: Nash proved that every finite game has...
o: At least one equilibrium in mixed strategies
A dominant strategy for every player
A pure strategy equilibrium without any mixing
A single unique equilibrium, and only one

questions.q: In the ultimatum game, why do real responders often reject low offers?
o: Fairness concerns matter beyond money
They misread the rules of the game
They actually want to receive less money
Their choices are random and have no pattern

o: Many outcomes, including cooperation, can be equilibria
Only defection is possible as an outcome

questions.q: Match each term to its meaning.
pairs: One player's gain is the other's loss
Players gain by choosing matching actions

questions.q: Explain why a penalty taker should randomise rather than always shoot to the same corner.
questions.model: If the taker is predictable the goalkeeper can exploit it by diving that way, so mixing makes it impossible to anticipate and is the equilibrium logic in a zero-sum game.

panel.q: In a one-shot ultimatum game with pot 10 and whole-unit offers, assume the responder accepts any positive offer and rejects an offer of 0. Backward induction (self-interested players) then predicts the proposer offers...
panel.why: The responder accepts any positive amount, so the proposer offers the smallest positive amount, 1, and keeps 9.

panel.q: Why might cooperation emerge in a repeated prisoner's dilemma but not in a one-shot version?
panel.model: In repeated play, defecting can be punished in future rounds and cooperation rewarded, so if players value the future enough, cooperating pays more than the one-time gain from defecting.

panel.q: An evolutionarily stable strategy is one that...
o: Cannot be invaded by a rare alternative
Is always the best outcome for the whole group
Uses only mixed strategies and never pure ones
Always wins against every other strategy
panel.why: Mutants do worse than the incumbent strategy.

teach.model: Mixed-strategy equilibria arise when no pure strategy is stable, as in matching pennies. Sequential games are solved by backward induction, and subgame perfection removes non-credible threats. Repeated games allow cooperation if players value the future enough, as the folk theorem states.

points.ask: How do I solve sequential games?

stages.title: Complex systems analysis
stages.hook: A tiny change in the starting value of a simple equation can produce completely different outcomes later. How can a simple rule produce such complex behaviour?
explain: A complex system has many interacting components whose collective behaviour cannot be easily read off from the parts. Key features: emergence (system-level patterns not present in any component), nonlinearity (effects not proportional to causes), feedback and adaptation, and sensitivity to initial conditions. Examples include ecosystems, economies, the climate, the brain and the internet.

Simple rules can give complex behaviour. The logistic map x(n+1) = r x(n) (1 − x(n)) shows this. For r = 2.5 the value settles at x = 1 − 1/r = 0.6; for r = 3.2 it oscillates between two values; for r near 3.9 it behaves chaotically, with sensitive dependence: nearby starts diverge exponentially. Chaos is deterministic yet hard to predict long term. With r = 3.2 and x0 = 0.5: x1 = 3.2 × 0.25 = 0.8 and x2 = 3.2 × 0.8 × 0.2 = 0.512.

Networks matter: in a complete network of n nodes there are n(n − 1)/2 links, so connections grow faster than nodes. Many networks have hubs (heavy-tailed degree distributions), which makes them robust to random failure but vulnerable to targeted attack on hubs. Tipping points and hysteresis can make changes abrupt and hard to reverse. Reinforcing growth at a rate g per period doubles in about ln 2 / ln(1 + g) periods (roughly 70/g%). Because prediction is limited, analysts use models for understanding scenarios and robustness, not exact forecasts, and watch for early warning signals such as critical slowing down.

example.q: Use the logistic map with r = 3.2 and x0 = 0.5 to find x2.

analogies.nature: Flocks of birds move in coordinated patterns from simple local rules without a leader (emergence).
analogies.city: Traffic jams emerge from many drivers' small braking decisions.
analogies.tech: Social networks spread information along hubs and links, so a few accounts have outsized reach.

A threshold beyond which the system shifts to a new state.
A node with many connections in a network.

misc.right: Chaotic systems are deterministic but tiny uncertainties grow exponentially, limiting prediction.

stages.limits: Complexity science mixes rigorous mathematics with loose analogies, so claims should be checked for evidence and not just metaphor.

teach.model: Complex systems show emergence, nonlinearity, feedback and sensitivity to starting conditions. Simple rules like the logistic map can give chaos. Networks have hubs and growing numbers of links. Tipping points and limits to prediction mean we use scenarios and look for early warnings.

stages.title: Strategic forecasting
stages.hook: Forecasters say there is a 70% chance of an event. It does not happen. Were they wrong?
explain: Strategic forecasting estimates future events to support decisions. A single probabilistic forecast cannot be judged right or wrong from one outcome; we assess forecasters over many predictions. Calibration means that of the events given 70%, about 70% happen. Resolution (or discrimination) means forecasts differ meaningfully from the base rate. A good forecaster is both calibrated and sharp.

The Brier score measures accuracy: the mean of (forecast − outcome)², where the outcome is 1 or 0. Lower is better; always saying 50% gives 0.25. For forecasts 0.9 (event occurred) and 0.3 (did not occur): (0.1² + 0.3²) ÷ 2 = (0.01 + 0.09) ÷ 2 = 0.05. Research by Philip Tetlock found that average experts were often only modestly better than simple benchmarks over long horizons, while some "superforecasters" achieved better accuracy through habits: start from base rates (the outside view, reference-class forecasting), break problems into parts (Fermi estimates), update in small steps on evidence, consider several perspectives, and keep score.

Methods include scenario planning (several coherent futures instead of one prediction), trend extrapolation with caution about regime changes, structured expert judgment (such as the Delphi method), prediction markets and aggregation (averaging independent forecasts usually beats most individuals). Limits: some systems are inherently unpredictable, rare events resist estimation, forecasts can change behaviour (self-fulfilling or self-defeating), and overconfidence and hindsight bias distort learning. Honest uncertainty ranges and clear definitions of what counts as the event improve usefulness.

example.q: Forecasts: 0.8 (event occurred), 0.6 (did not occur), 0.2 (did not occur), 0.9 (occurred). Compute the Brier score.

analogies.farm: A farmer starts from the base rate of rainy seasons before adjusting for this year's signs.
analogies.sport: A coach compares a team to all similar teams in the past rather than only its own story.
analogies.city: A city council plans for three scenarios of population growth rather than one.

stages.mnemonic: Start with the base, break it down, nudge with proof, keep score for the truth.
terms: Agreement between stated probabilities and actual frequencies.
Mean squared error of probability forecasts; lower is better.
A set of similar past cases used to set a base rate.
A coherent story about how the future might unfold.

misc.wrong: A forecaster who gave 70% to an event that did not happen was wrong.
misc.right: One outcome cannot judge a probability. Accuracy is judged over many forecasts by calibration and score.

stages.limits: Evidence on the accuracy of experts and of superforecasters comes from particular tournaments, and what holds for geopolitics or years ahead may not hold elsewhere.

trip.prompt: Find the habits associated with accurate forecasting.

teach.model: Forecasting is judged over many forecasts by calibration and score, not one outcome. Start from base rates, break problems into parts, update gradually, aggregate perspectives and keep score. Use scenarios for deep uncertainty. Some events are unpredictable, and forecasts can change behaviour.

stages.title: Rational belief revision
stages.hook: New evidence contradicts something you firmly believe. How should you change your mind, and by how much?
explain: Rational belief revision concerns how to update beliefs when evidence arrives. In the Bayesian account, beliefs are probabilities that should satisfy the probability axioms (coherence), and on learning evidence E for certain, you update by conditionalisation: P_new(H) = P(H | E). The justification for coherence includes Dutch book arguments: an agent with incoherent betting prices can be led to accept a set of bets that guarantees a loss. For example, pricing a 1-unit bet on A at 0.6 and on not-A at 0.6 (sum 1.2) means paying 1.2 for bets that together return exactly 1, a sure loss of 0.2.

Example of conditionalisation: P(H) = 0.3, P(E | H) = 0.8, P(E | not H) = 0.2. P(E) = 0.8 × 0.3 + 0.2 × 0.7 = 0.24 + 0.14 = 0.38. So P(H | E) = 0.24 ÷ 0.38 ≈ 0.632. If evidence is uncertain, Jeffrey conditionalisation generalises the rule. The AGM theory of belief revision (Alchourrón, Gärdenfors, Makinson) treats qualitative revision of belief sets with postulates such as minimal change and consistency. Calibration and avoiding extreme credences (0 or 1) keep you open to learning.

Disagreement among rational people: Aumann's agreement theorem says that ideally rational agents with common priors and common knowledge of their posteriors cannot agree to disagree; real disagreement involves different priors, private evidence, or limits of rationality, and the epistemology of peer disagreement debates whether to conciliate or hold firm. Practical habits: keep track of why you believe, set conditions that would change your mind in advance, change confidence in proportion to evidence strength, watch for motivated reasoning (evidence for a general backfire effect, where correction strengthens a belief, is mixed), and distinguish updating from social conformity. Memory limits matter here too: we misremember what we once believed (hindsight bias), so writing down predictions helps honest revision.

example.q: P(H) = 0.3, P(E | H) = 0.8, P(E | not H) = 0.2. Find P(H | E).

analogies.sport: A scout updates a rating after each match by an amount that matches how informative the match is.
analogies.tech: A model updates its estimate of a user's preference with each click.
analogies.nature: A scientist revises a hypothesis about a species' range after new field records.

stages.mnemonic: Weigh by the proof, shift by the ratio, record what you thought so you know.
terms: Updating the probability of a hypothesis to its probability given the evidence.
Having degrees of belief that obey the probability axioms.
A set of bets guaranteeing a loss for an incoherent agent.
A formal theory of qualitative belief revision.

misc.right: Updating in proportion to evidence is rational; refusing to update is the failure.

stages.limits: Bayesian updating needs well-defined priors and likelihoods, which are difficult to specify, and the theory of disagreement and of revision with new concepts remains open.

teach.model: Rational updating follows probability: conditionalise on evidence, keep credences coherent and avoid certainty about empirical claims. Dutch book arguments support coherence. Disagreement stems from differing priors, information and limits. Record predictions to resist hindsight.

stages.title: Integrated knowledge and strategy challenge
stages.hook: You need to master a hard subject in six months, make good decisions along the way and judge conflicting claims. How do you integrate everything you have learned about thinking?
explain: This capstone integrates the strands of the world. Reasoning: deduce carefully, generalise cautiously, choose the best explanation, and check arguments for validity, soundness and fallacies. Evidence: ask about sources, design, base rates, confounders and replication. Uncertainty: express beliefs as probabilities, update them by Bayes' rule, and weigh risk. Decisions and strategy: define goals and constraints, compare options by expected utility, plan for scenarios, and use game-theoretic thinking when others respond.

Learning itself is an application. Evidence-based techniques: retrieval practice (testing yourself), spaced practice (spreading sessions over time), interleaving (mixing problem types), elaboration and self-explanation, and teaching others. Memory palaces (the method of loci) use familiar places as hooks and work well for ordered lists, but they do not help understanding by themselves. Limits matter: forgetting is fast without review (the forgetting curve of Ebbinghaus); memories are reconstructed, so false memories can feel vivid; the misinformation effect shows that later suggestion can alter recall; and confidence is only loosely linked to accuracy. Practising a brain-training game improves that game, but good evidence for broad transfer to general intelligence is lacking.

Metacognition ties it together: monitor your understanding with tests rather than feelings of familiarity, set review schedules, reflect on mistakes, and calibrate confidence through feedback. Intellectual humility, charity toward opposing views, and willingness to revise are habits as important as technique. Knowledge is collective: we rely on institutions, testimony and expert communities, so evaluating sources and understanding expert disagreement are core skills. A wise thinker also knows when not to compute: some decisions turn on values, not calculations.

example.q: A test is 95% sensitive with 10% false positives for a condition with 2% prevalence. A student tests positive. What is the chance they have it, and what would you do next?
steps: Per 1000: 20 have it, 19 test positive; 980 do not, 98 test positive.
Next step: a more specific confirmatory test, since P is only about 16%.
example.a: About 16%; do a confirmatory test rather than assuming the condition.

analogies.farm: A farmer uses records over years (base rates), experiments with plots (fair tests) and several scenarios for the weather.
analogies.music: A musician practises with spacing and mixing, tests herself in performance and learns from mistakes.
analogies.city: A planner combines data, models, stakeholder views and review points for a transport scheme.

terms: Matching confidence to the frequency of being right.

stages.limits: The evidence for learning techniques is strong on average but varies across tasks and learners, and the effects of general "thinking skills" training on unrelated tasks are modest and debated.

teach.model: Integrate reasoning, evidence, probability, decisions and strategy. Learn with spaced retrieval and mixed practice, remember that forgetting, false memory and overconfidence are real, and brain games do not reliably raise general intelligence. Stay humble and review.
